_metadata.notice: ESTIMATE ONLY - 30-day onboarding milestones structured around the 3-3-3 rule for rescue adoptions in India.

tasks.title: Establish Safe Zone & Quiet Decompression
tasks.description: Set up a calm, quiet corner with bed, clean water, and chew toy. Do not invite guests or throw welcome parties; let your pet decompress.

tasks.title: Veterinary Health Assessment & Microchip Registration
tasks.description: Visit a verified neighborhood clinic for baseline physical examination, deworming verification, and municipal pet license initiation.

tasks.title: Predictable Feeding & Potty Schedule
tasks.description: Take puppy or adult dog out every 3 hours and right after meals. Reward immediately with positive praise when they relieve outside.

tasks.title: Apartment Acclimatization & Elevator Training
tasks.description: Introduce elevator sounds, corridor echoes, and society gate staff gently with high-value treats to prevent reactive barking.

tasks.title: Separation Tolerance & Crate Comfort
tasks.description: Practice leaving the apartment for 15, 30, and 60 minutes increments to build confidence and avoid separation distress.

tasks.title: Long Leash Walks & Basic Recall Commands
tasks.description: Solidify 'Sit', 'Stay', and 'Come' commands in quiet outdoor parks. Ensure double-clip harness for Indian street safety.

tasks.title: Sanctuary Room Confinement
tasks.description: Keep your new cat in a single quiet room with litter box, food, scratching post, and hiding hideout before whole-house access.

tasks.title: Balcony & Window Safety Net Inspection
tasks.description: Verify high-density pigeon/safety netting across all balconies and sliding windows before expanding home territory.

tasks.title: Gradual Room-by-Room Home Exploration
tasks.description: Open doors gradually during calm evening hours. Place vertical scratchers and pheromone diffusers along hallway paths.

tasks.title: Grooming Desensitization & Carrier Training
tasks.description: Leave carrier open with blanket and treats so carrier is seen as a cozy nap spot rather than a vet trauma trigger.
